title: Snapshot Telescope — Bisect Heuristics & Canary Comparison Playbook
content:
Summary:
A compact field playbook for using the 'Snapshot Telescope' approach when tracking down performance regressions during canary runs and alert triage. Focus is on practical heuristics for choosing bisect checkpoints, quick profiler captures that don't destroy canary signal, and dashboard queries to triangulate root cause within 1–3 hours.

Context / motivation:
- We often get noisy latency spikes in canaries where metrics diverge but the cause is unclear (model variant change, kernel/driver update, autoscaler behavior, or traffic shaping).
- Full bisects (binary search over many commits) are expensive and slow. The Snapshot Telescope approach compresses the search space by comparing short, time-aligned snapshots of traces/metrics across candidate deltas.
- This doc codifies heuristics we use in the runtime team when we need a fast verdict (will this rollout kill the SLA?) and a reproducible artifact for post-mortem.

When to use Snapshot Telescope:
- Canary shows >5% P99 regression or >10% cost-per-token increase in first 30 minutes.
- Alert triggered without obvious infra noise (no obvious host OOM/driver crash).
- You need a quick human-parsable comparison to decide rollback vs keep-testing.

High-level steps (cheat-sheet):
1) Capture a synchronized snapshot window (2–5 minutes) of:
   - Traces (sampled traces for requests in canary),
   - Token-level timing/kv-cache stats,
   - Host GPU metrics (util, mem, SM busy),
   - Model-serving runtime counters (batch sizes, queue depth),
   - Routing/fallback logs.
2) Pull the same window from a healthy baseline canary (either last green canary in same cluster or a pinned baseline instance).
3) Run lightweight profile artifacts: CPU perf counters (5s), CUDA nvprof-lite (if available, 5s), and a single process-level PyTorch op timeline snapshot (if model is PyTorch-based).
4) Compute diffs for: median/95/99 latency, token throughput, kv-cache hit ratio, average batch size, kernel execution time percentiles.
5) If diffs point to kernel/driver/host issue, escalate to infra SRE with artifacts. If diffs point to model variant (increased token churn, degraded kv-cache hit), consider immediate rollback.

Bisect heuristics (practical):
- Prefer commit-range shrinking by 'behavioral' anchors, not pure chronological order. Anchors = last-known-good canary, first-canary-with-regression, any infrastructure change (driver, CUDA, kernel) in the window.
- If there are >8 candidate commits, create 3-way snapshot comparisons: baseline vs midpoint vs failing. This often reveals which half contains the delta without running 8 full canaries.
- Use feature flags/pinned-config diffs (rollout staging flags) as extra anchors. Sometimes config flips are the root cause.

Canary comparison checklist (rapid):
- Basic sanity: identical traffic profile, same input distribution sample (seeded requests), same routing policy.
- Metrics to plot immediate diffs: P50/P95/P99 latency, requests/sec, average batch size, kv-cache hit%, GPU SM utilization, GPU memcpy time, open file/socket counts.
- Collect one zipped artifact containing: traces.json.gz, flamegraphs/agg.svg, nvtx timeline, runtime-counters.json. Attach to incident ticket.

Dashboard queries (examples to copy):
- P99 latency by model_variant: rate(metric_request_latency{model=~".*"}) or PromQL equivalent.
- Avg batch size over time: avg_over_time(runtime_batch_size[5m]) grouped by pool.
- KV cache efficiency: sum(kv_hits) / sum(kv_lookups) by model, 5m window.
- Kernel skew: 95th percentile of kernel_exec_ms by gpu_id.
(If you need exact PromQL snippets, see CONFLUENCE-ServRuntime-SnapshotTelescope)

Lightweight profiling commands (keep canary alive):
- trace-sampler --duration 5s --rate 1/50 --out trace.json (samples only).
- nvprof-lite --pid <server_pid> --time 5 --out nvtx.json (if allowed by infra).
- collect-flame --process <pid> --duration 3 --format collapsed > flame.collapsed
Note: avoid long-running profilers on canary; prefer 3–10s bursts repeated across windows to gather statistically useful samples.

Interpreting common patterns (quick heuristics):
- Increased memcpy time + GPU low SM utilization => data transfer bottleneck (PCIe / NVLink / PCIe driver). Check kernel/driver and host NUMA.
- Higher per-token op time but similar batch sizes => model op regression (new kernel or quant change).
- Larger median batch size but increased P99 => queuing/backpressure from a downstream shard or NACK/retry behavior.
- KV-cache hit% drop with matching latency jump => model caching behavior or prompt prefix change; check prompt routing and input dedup.

Escalation path (1–3 hour remediation target):
- 0–30m: owner runs Snapshot Telescope, collects artifacts, decides rollback if >20% P99 regression.
- 30–90m: if inconclusive and customers impacted, run targeted bisect (3-way midpoint) and request infra trace captures.
- 90–180m: escalate to eng+SRE war-room, freeze rollouts for the affected model variant, start full binary bisect if required.

Artifacts to attach when filing ticket:
- Two time-aligned trace exports (baseline + failing).
- Aggregated flamegraphs (svg) for both states.
- Runtime counters json (batch sizes, queue depth, kv stats).
- Short profiler captures (nvtx, perf) and their timestamps.
- Screenshot of dashboard diffs (P99, kv hit, batch size).

Open questions / TODOs:
- (TODO) Automate snapshot alignment across regions (timestamps drift). See INFRA-4821 for clock-sync work.
- (TODO) Add a lightweight in-proxy sampler that adds KV-cache tagging to traces (Samantha ownership).
- (Question) Should we standardize 5s nvprof-lite as default or let SRE opt-in? Pros/cons in thread: slack://channel/perf-hunters/thread/GB12KQ9Q8

Notes from last run (2026-01-10 canary):
- Observed 18% P99 increase coincident with kernel 51091 driver rollout. Snapshot Telescope diff showed memcpy 95th increase of 3.2x and GPU SM util drop vs baseline. Root cause: driver regression (rolled back by infra). Artifacts attached to INFRA-4821.

Quick decision guide (one-sentence each):
- If memcpy %t rises sharply -> escalate to infra (driver/host).
- If op execution time rises without memcopy changes -> revert model variant or quant change.
- If kv-cache hit falls -> investigate prompt distribution and routing.
- If batch size skew appears -> look for downstream backpressure and request shaping.

Appendix (examples to paste into ticket):
- Incident title template: "[Snapshot-Telescope] <model> P99 +X% during canary — candidate: <commit/driver>"
- Minimal artifact list: traces.json.gz, flame.svg, runtime-counters.json, short-nvtx.zip

If you're oncall and want a faster walk-through, ping me (Asha) or @Diego in perf-hunters. I can walk through a live example in 15–20 minutes.

-- end of notes --
